title: Hosting Thanksgiving With ADHD: A Low-Stress Plan From Fridge to Leftovers
description: Hosting Thanksgiving with a busy brain? A simple countdown, a clean-enough house plan and tricks for the day itself, from timers to the leftover station.
intro:
Hosting Thanksgiving with an ADHD brain can feel like running a restaurant, a hotel and a cleaning company at the same time, all while making small talk with your aunt.

The food has five different timers. The house needs to look like adults live there. And somewhere in all of it, you're meant to relax and be grateful.

Here's the good news: you don't need to be a natural host. You need a plan that lives on paper instead of in your head. This one breaks Thanksgiving into small jobs across two weeks, with a clean-enough house plan and a day-of setup that does the remembering for you.

sections.heading: Decide your 'good enough' Thanksgiving
sections.body:
Before planning anything, write down the three things that matter most to you. Maybe it's the turkey, Grandma's stuffing and everyone around one table. Everything else is a bonus.

Then decide what you can hand off. Ask guests to bring sides, drinks or dessert. Buy the rolls. Use paper plates for dessert. Every handed-off job is energy you get to keep for the day.

sections.heading: Two weeks out: the menu and the list
sections.body:
In one sitting, write the menu and turn it straight into a shopping list. Group the list by store section so you aren't zigzagging through aisles.

Buy shelf-stable things this week: broth, canned pumpkin, foil, napkins, drinks. The last-minute shop gets much smaller, and smaller lists are easier to finish.

sections.heading: One week out: clear the fridge
sections.body:
This is the step everyone forgets until there's a 15-pound turkey and nowhere to put it. Spend 10 minutes clearing old leftovers and half-empty jars. Eat from the fridge and freezer this week so there's room.

While you're there, check that you have enough serving dishes, spoons and a roasting pan. Put a sticky note on each dish with what's going in it. Day-of you will be so grateful.

sections.heading: The clean-enough house plan
sections.body:
Guests only see a few spots. Focus on those and close the doors on the rest:

- **Entry:** clear the floor and make room for coats.
- **Guest bathroom:** wipe the counter, fresh towel, extra toilet paper where people can see it.
- **Living room:** clear surfaces, fluff the pillows.
- **Dining table:** off with the mail pile (into a box is fine).

Do one zone a night for the four nights before. 15 minutes each, then stop.

sections.heading: The day before: set the table
sections.body:
Set the table the night before, down to the napkins. Chill the drinks. Make anything that tastes fine reheated: cranberry sauce, pies, casseroles you'll bake tomorrow.

Then write the **day-of timeline**. Work backward from dinner time and write every oven time on one sheet. "1:00 turkey in. 4:30 turkey out to rest. 4:40 stuffing and sweet potatoes in." Tape it to a cabinet at eye level.

sections.heading: On the day: let timers hold the details
sections.body:
Our working memory runs out fast when the kitchen is loud and people keep asking where the bathroom is. So don't try to remember the oven.

Set a separate named timer on your phone or smart speaker for each dish: "turkey baste," "rolls in." Glance at the timeline when one goes off. If someone offers to help, give them a specific job off the list. "Can you mash the potatoes?" is easier for everyone than "Oh, I'm fine."

sections.heading: Set up a leftover station
sections.body:
Before dinner, set out containers, foil, a marker and a roll of masking tape on one counter. After dinner, guests can pack their own plates to take home, and you can label what's left with the date.

This turns the after-dinner chaos into a self-serve line, and it means fewer dishes left behind for you.

sections.heading: Cleanup: the 20-minute rule
sections.body:
After the meal, do 20 minutes of cleanup max, then stop. Food in the fridge, trash out, dishwasher running. The roasting pan can soak overnight. Nothing about Thanksgiving cleanup needs to be finished the same night.

And please, sit down at some point. You earned it.

outro:
A good Thanksgiving isn't the one with the spotless house or the perfect pie. It's the one where you're still standing at the end and maybe even enjoyed some of it. Put the plan on paper, hand off what you can and let timers do the remembering.

If you like a printed checklist on the fridge, the *Tidy Brain Printable Pack* has countdown and cleaning pages you can use for any holiday you host.
